learningAid.title: Prefix Sum Algorithm
learningAid.explanation: By storing the cumulative sum of elements from the start up to each index, the sum of a specific range [l, r] can be found by taking the total sum up to r and subtracting the sum that occurred before l.

hints: Instead of calculating the sum for every query from scratch, can you reuse work done for previous indices?
Think about storing a running total (cumulative sum) so that you don't need to recompute sums repeatedly.
If you store prefix sums, you can get range sum using: sum(l, r) = prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]
common_mistakes: Using prefix[r] - prefix[l] instead of prefix[r+1] - prefix[l]
Not creating n+1 size array → leads to messy edge cases
Breaks calculations when l = 0
Missing the whole point → ends up O(n) per query
Not being clear whether r is included or excluded
content.problem_description: Given an integer array nums, handle multiple queries of the following type: Calculate the sum of the elements of nums between indices left and right inclusive where left <= right.

hints: Each row starts and ends with 1.
Every element (except the edges) is the sum of the two elements in the row above it.
Build row by row, using the previous row to compute the current row.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add 1s at the start and end of each row
Off-by-one errors when indexing into the previous row
Not initializing the first row as [1]
content.problem_description: Given an integer numRows, return the first numRows of Pascal's triangle. In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it.

problems.name: Largest Subarray with K Sum (Prefix Sum + Hashmap)

hints: Compute prefix sums as you traverse the array.
At each index, check if (prefix_sum - K) has been seen before.
Store the first occurrence index of each prefix sum in a hashmap.
common_mistakes: Updating the hashmap before checking leads to wrong results
Not initializing hashmap with {0: -1} for subarrays starting at index 0
Confusing this with the subarray sum equals K count problem
content.problem_description: Given an array of integers and a target sum K, find the length of the longest subarray whose sum equals K.

hints: Instead of updating every element in a range, use a difference array to mark range starts and ends.
Build prefix sums of the difference array to get actual decrements at each position.
Check if each element can be decremented to 0 without going negative.
common_mistakes: Off-by-one: difference array update at r+1 instead of r
Not reconstructing actual values via prefix sum before checking
Trying brute-force for large inputs — TLE guaranteed
content.problem_description: Given an array nums and a list of queries [l, r, val], apply the operation: decrement all elements in the range [l, r] by val. Check if the array can be made all zeros.

hints: Since the array is sorted, use two pointers — one at the start, one at the end.
If the sum is too large, move the right pointer left. If too small, move left pointer right.
The sorted property guarantees you won't miss valid pairs.
common_mistakes: Using the same element twice
Not leveraging the sorted property (using hashmap wastes space)
Off-by-one on 1-indexed return values
content.problem_description: Given a 1-indexed sorted array of integers, find two numbers that add up to a specific target. Return their indices.

hints: Maintain three pointers: low, mid, and high.
Elements before low are 0s; between low and mid are 1s; after high are 2s.
Process elements at mid: swap with low if 0, keep if 1, swap with high if 2.
common_mistakes: Incrementing mid after swapping with high — the swapped element is unprocessed
Not initializing pointers correctly
Using extra space when O(1) is required
content.problem_description: Given an array with values 0, 1, and 2 (representing red, white, and blue), sort them in-place so that all 0s come first, then 1s, then 2s.

hints: Start filling from the end of nums1 to avoid overwriting unprocessed elements.
Use three pointers: one at end of nums1's valid part (m-1), one at end of nums2 (n-1), one at the last position (m+n-1).
Always place the larger of the two current elements at the current end position.
common_mistakes: Merging from the front overwrites elements you haven't processed yet
Forgetting to handle remaining elements in nums2 after nums1 is exhausted
content.problem_description: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2, merge nums2 into nums1 in-place. nums1 has extra space at the end to accommodate nums2.

hints: Use a slow pointer to mark the position of the last unique element.
Use a fast pointer to scan through the array.
When fast pointer finds a new unique element, place it at the slow pointer position.
common_mistakes: Returning count instead of the right k value
Not starting slow pointer at index 1 (first element is always unique)
content.problem_description: Given a sorted array, remove the duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears only once. Return the number of unique elements.

hints: Maintain a running count of consecutive 1s and a max count.
Reset running count to 0 when you encounter a 0.
Update max count at every step.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to update the max before resetting the counter
Not checking the final count after the loop ends
content.problem_description: Given a binary array nums, return the maximum number of consecutive 1s in the array.

hints: Sort the array first to enable two-pointer technique and easy duplicate skipping.
Fix one element i, then use two pointers (left = i+1, right = end) for the remaining.
Skip duplicate values of i, left, and right to avoid duplicate triplets.
common_mistakes: Not skipping duplicates after finding a valid triplet
Not moving both left and right when a triplet is found
Using nested loops without the two-pointer trick (TLE)
content.problem_description: Given an integer array nums, return all triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i != j, i != k, j != k, and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0.

hints: Extend 3Sum: fix two elements with two loops, then use two pointers for the rest.
Sort first; skip duplicates at each of the two fixed positions.
Be careful with overflow for large targets — use long long.
common_mistakes: Integer overflow when summing four large numbers
Duplicate skipping logic applied incorrectly
Forgetting to skip duplicates at both the outer and inner fixed loops
content.problem_description: Given an array nums and a target, return all unique quadruplets [nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]] that sum to target.

hints: Use a slow pointer tracking where the next non-zero should go.
On each non-zero element, place it at the slow pointer and advance both.
Fill remaining positions from slow pointer to end with 0.
common_mistakes: Swapping instead of overwriting (can work but adds unnecessary operations)
Not zeroing out the tail after placing non-zeros
content.problem_description: Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end of it while maintaining the relative order of non-zero elements.

hints: Water at any index is min(maxLeft, maxRight) - height[i].
Precompute max heights from left and right with prefix/suffix arrays.
Optimize to O(1) space: use two pointers moving inward; the smaller side determines water.
common_mistakes: Not accounting for negative water (use max(0, ...)
Two-pointer: forgetting to update maxLeft/maxRight before computing water
content.problem_description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.

hints: Use a modified merge sort: count pairs across left and right halves before merging.
During the count phase, use two pointers across sorted halves.
The merge step then proceeds normally.
common_mistakes: Counting pairs during merge instead of before merge (wrong results)
Confusing this with count of inversions (condition is > 2*j not > j)
content.problem_description: Given an integer array nums, return the number of reverse pairs. A reverse pair is a pair (i, j) where i < j and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j].

hints: Start with pointers at both ends (leftmost and rightmost lines).
At each step, move the pointer pointing to the shorter line inward.
The area is limited by the shorter line, so moving the taller one cannot increase the area.
Keep track of the maximum area seen so far.
common_mistakes: Moving both pointers inward instead of just the shorter one
Not correctly calculating area as min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)
Missing edge cases when pointers meet
Starting pointers from the same side instead of opposite ends
content.problem_description: You are given an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the ith line are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]). Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

hints: Use two pointers: one at the start, one at the end.
Skip non-alphanumeric characters while moving pointers.
Compare characters at both pointers after converting to lowercase.
Move pointers toward each other until they meet.
common_mistakes: Not handling case sensitivity properly
Not skipping non-alphanumeric characters correctly
Using extra space when O(1) is possible
Off-by-one errors in pointer movement
content.problem_description: Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome, or false otherwise. A string is a palindrome if it reads the same forward and backward after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters.

learningAid.title: Sliding Window Technique
learningAid.explanation: The sliding window technique maintains a window of fixed or variable size that slides through the array. Instead of recalculating everything for each window, we update incrementally by adding new elements and removing old ones, achieving O(n) time complexity.

problems.name: Find the Power of K-Size Subarrays I

hints: For each window of size k, count the frequency of the maximum element.
Use a sliding window approach to efficiently update the maximum and its count.
Maintain a frequency map of elements in the current window.
When sliding, decrement count of outgoing element and increment for incoming.
common_mistakes: Not correctly handling duplicate maximums in the window
Recalculating the maximum for each window from scratch
Off-by-one errors in window boundaries
Not updating the frequency map correctly when sliding
content.problem_description: You are given an array of integers nums of length n and a positive integer k. The power of a subarray is the number of times the subarray's maximum appears in that subarray. Return the sum of the power of all subarrays of nums having length k.

hints: Use a sliding window with left and right pointers.
Maintain a hashmap of character to its most recent index.
When you find a duplicate, move left pointer to max of current left and duplicate index + 1.
Track the maximum window size seen.
common_mistakes: Not updating left pointer correctly when duplicate is found
Moving left pointer to duplicate index instead of duplicate index + 1
Not using max() when updating left pointer (can move backwards)
Forgetting to update the hashmap with new character positions
content.problem_description: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.

hints: Use a sliding window that expands when sum < target and shrinks when sum >= target.
Maintain the minimum window length that satisfies the condition.
Since all numbers are positive, shrinking the window can only decrease the sum.
Track the starting position of the current window.
common_mistakes: Not handling the case when no valid subarray exists
Not shrinking the window optimally (missing smaller valid windows)
Using wrong condition for window expansion/shrinking
Not updating the minimum length correctly
content.problem_description: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target. If there is no such subarray, return 0.

problems.name: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K (Monotonic Queue)

hints: Compute prefix sums first.
Use a monotonic queue to store indices of increasing prefix sums.
For each index, pop from queue while prefix sum difference >= k.
Maintain queue in increasing order of prefix sums for optimal results.
common_mistakes: Using regular sliding window (doesn't work with negative numbers)
Not maintaining monotonic property of the queue
Incorrectly handling the prefix sum calculations
Not updating the answer correctly when finding valid subarrays
content.problem_description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the length of the shortest non-empty subarray whose sum is at least k. If there is no such subarray, return -1. Note: The array can contain negative numbers.

hints: Use a deque that stores indices in decreasing order of their values.
Remove indices from front if they're outside the current window.
Remove indices from back if their values are <= current element.
The front of the deque always contains the maximum for the current window.
common_mistakes: Not removing elements that are outside the window bounds
Not maintaining the decreasing order property
Using heap instead of deque (less efficient)
Storing values instead of indices (can't check window bounds)
content.problem_description: You are given an array of integers nums and an integer k. A sliding window of size k moves from the left to right. Return the max sliding window for each window position.

hints: Use the formula: subarrays with exactly K = subarrays with at most K - subarrays with at most K-1.
For 'at most K', use a sliding window with a frequency map.
Expand right pointer, shrink left when distinct count > K.
Count all valid windows for each right pointer position.
common_mistakes: Trying to directly count 'exactly K' instead of using the formula
Not correctly updating the frequency map when sliding
Off-by-one errors in window counting
Not handling edge cases when K = 1
content.problem_description: Given an array of positive integers nums and an integer k, return the number of subarrays where the number of distinct integers in that subarray is exactly k.

hints: Treat each row as a histogram of heights (consecutive 1s from top).
For each row, calculate the largest rectangle in histogram.
Use monotonic stack to find largest rectangle in histogram in O(n).
Build heights incrementally by adding 1 from previous row if current cell is 1.
common_mistakes: Not correctly building the histogram heights for each row
Using wrong algorithm for largest rectangle in histogram
Not resetting heights when encountering a 0 in the matrix
Complex stack implementation errors
content.problem_description: Given a rows x cols binary matrix filled with 0's and 1's, find the largest rectangle containing only 1's and return its area.

problems.name: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K

hints: Calculate sum of first k elements as the initial window sum.
Slide the window by subtracting the element going out and adding the element coming in.
Keep track of the maximum sum seen during the sliding process.
This technique works because we're maintaining a fixed-size window.
common_mistakes: Recalculating the sum for each window from scratch
Off-by-one errors in window boundaries
Not handling edge cases when array length < k
Forgetting to update the maximum after each slide
content.problem_description: Given an array of integers and a number k, find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size k.

problems.name: First Negative in Every Window of Size K

hints: Use a deque to store indices of negative numbers in the current window.
Remove indices from front that are outside the current window.
The front of the deque always contains the first negative in the window.
If deque is empty, there's no negative in the current window.
common_mistakes: Not removing indices that are outside the window bounds
Storing values instead of indices (can't check window bounds)
Not handling the case when there are no negatives in a window
Using regular sliding window instead of deque for this pattern
content.problem_description: Given an array of integers and a window size k, find the first negative number in every window of size k. If there is no negative number in a window, output 0 for that window.

learningAid.title: Interval Merging & Sorting
learningAid.explanation: The key to interval problems is sorting intervals by start time. This allows linear-time merging and comparison. For overlapping intervals, always compare the current interval's start with the last merged interval's end. This pattern applies to most interval problems.

hints: Sort intervals by their start time.
Compare each interval with the last merged interval.
If current interval's start <= last merged's end, they overlap - merge them.
If no overlap, add current interval to merged list as-is.
common_mistakes: Not sorting intervals first (cannot merge in O(n) without sorting)
Updating end incorrectly - should use max of both ends
Not handling edge case of empty input
Creating new intervals instead of modifying existing ones
content.problem_description: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

hints: Find the position where new interval should be inserted.
Merge overlapping intervals while traversing.
Keep track of intervals that end before new interval starts.
Handle intervals that start after new interval ends separately.
common_mistakes: Not handling cases where new interval doesn't overlap with any existing intervals
Not correctly merging intervals that overlap with new interval
Creating unnecessary new arrays instead of modifying in place
Off-by-one errors in interval comparisons
content.problem_description: You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start time, and a new interval. Insert the new interval into the array and merge if necessary. Return the array after insertion.

hints: Use two pointers, one for each list.
Compare the end of each interval to find overlaps.
If intervals overlap, add intersection to result.
Move the pointer that ends first to explore more possibilities.
common_mistakes: Not correctly calculating intersection start and end
Not handling cases where intervals don't overlap
Moving both pointers simultaneously instead of the one that ends first
Complex logic for intersection calculation
content.problem_description: You are given two lists of closed intervals where each list is disjoint and sorted by start time. Return the intersection of the two lists.

hints: Sort intervals by end time (not start time).
Greedily select intervals that don't overlap with the last selected.
Count how many intervals you can keep, answer = total - kept.
The greedy approach works because sorting by end gives optimal local choices.
common_mistakes: Sorting by start time instead of end time (greedy fails)
Not handling the case when intervals just touch at endpoints
Counting removals instead of keeping track of kept intervals
Using DP when greedy is sufficient and more efficient
content.problem_description: Given an array of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest of the intervals non-overlapping.

hints: Sort intervals by start time.
Check if any meeting starts before the previous meeting ends.
If any overlap found, return false.
If no overlaps after checking all, return true.
common_mistakes: Not sorting intervals first
Comparing wrong intervals (should compare current with previous)
Not handling edge case of single meeting
Using end time for sorting instead of start time
content.problem_description: Given an array of meeting time intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], determine if a person could attend all meetings.

hints: Sort meetings by start time.
Use a min heap to track end times of ongoing meetings.
When a meeting starts, remove all meetings that have ended from heap.
Push current meeting end time to heap, track max heap size.
common_mistakes: Not sorting meetings by start time
Using wrong heap property (should be min heap on end times)
Not cleaning up ended meetings from heap
Counting overlaps instead of concurrent meetings
content.problem_description: Given an array of meeting time intervals, return the minimum number of conference rooms required to accommodate all meetings without overlap.

learningAid.title: Matrix Traversal & Manipulation
learningAid.explanation: Matrix traversal problems often involve careful boundary management. Use four pointers (top, bottom, left, right) to track current bounds. Process in order: top row, right column, bottom row, left column. Always check bounds after each direction to avoid duplicate processing.

hints: Use four boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
Traverse top row left to right, then increment top.
Traverse right column top to bottom, then decrement right.
Traverse bottom row right to left, then decrement bottom.
Traverse left column bottom to top, then increment left.
Check boundary conditions after each traversal.
common_mistakes: Not checking boundary conditions after each direction
Processing same elements twice when matrix is not square
Forgetting to increment/decrement boundaries after each pass
Incorrect loop conditions for non-square matrices
content.problem_description: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order (clockwise, starting from top-left corner).

hints: The matrix can be treated as a sorted 1D array.
Map 1D index to 2D coordinates: row = idx / n, col = idx % n.
Perform standard binary search on the virtual 1D array.
Alternatively, binary search on first column to find row, then binary search within that row.
common_mistakes: Not correctly mapping 1D index to 2D coordinates
Using O(m*n) space to flatten the matrix
Doing linear search instead of binary search
Not leveraging the sorted property of both rows and columns
content.problem_description: Write an efficient algorithm that searches for a value in an m x n matrix where each row is sorted in ascending order and the first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row.

hints: Use first row and first column as marker arrays.
Use two separate flags to track if first row/col should be zeroed.
First pass: mark zeros using first row/col.
Second pass: set zeros based on markers (except first row/col).
Finally, set first row/col based on flags.
common_mistakes: Not handling first row and column separately (they are the markers)
Setting zeros during first pass (cascading zeros)
Using O(m*n) extra space when O(1) is possible
Forgetting to process the marker rows/columns at the end
content.problem_description: Given an m x n matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it in-place.

hints: Method 1: Transpose matrix, then reverse each row.
Method 2: Process layer by layer from outside in.
For layer-by-layer: swap four elements in a cycle.
Remember: clockwise rotation = transpose + reverse rows.
Counter-clockwise = transpose + reverse columns.
common_mistakes: Using extra space when in-place is required
Doing transpose incorrectly (swapping both i,j and j,i)
Forgetting to reverse after transpose for clockwise rotation
Incorrect layer boundary calculations in layer-by-layer approach
content.problem_description: Given an n x n matrix, rotate it by 90 degrees clockwise in-place.

learningAid.title: Hash Map Frequency Counting
learningAid.explanation: Hash maps provide O(1) average time for insert, delete, and lookup. Use them to count frequencies, check existence, or store key-value pairs. For frequency problems, count occurrences first, then iterate through the map to find patterns (duplicates, most frequent, etc.).

hints: Use a hashmap to count occurrences of each number.
The number with count 2 is the repeating number.
The number with count 0 is the missing number.
For O(1) space, use the mathematical approach: sum and sum of squares.
common_mistakes: Using O(n²) bruteforce instead of hashmap
Not handling edge cases when repeating or missing is at boundaries
Forgetting to check both repeating and missing in the same pass
Using wrong formula in mathematical approach
content.problem_description: Given an array of size N containing numbers from 1 to N, find the repeating and missing numbers. One number appears twice, one is missing.

problems.name: Find the Duplicate in an Array of N+1 Integers (Cycle Detection)

hints: Treat array values as pointers to next indices (like a linked list).
Since values are between 1 and n, there must be a cycle.
Use Floyd's algorithm: slow moves by 1, fast moves by 2 to find cycle.
After finding cycle, find the start of cycle (duplicate).
common_mistakes: Using extra space when constant space is required
Modifying the array when it should remain unchanged
Not correctly implementing Floyd's cycle detection
Off-by-one errors in index calculations
content.problem_description: Given an array of n+1 integers where each integer is between 1 and n inclusive, prove that at least one duplicate exists. Find the duplicate without modifying the array and using constant space.

hints: Use a hash set to store all numbers for O(1) lookup.
For each number, check if it's the start of a sequence (num-1 not in set).
If it's a start, count consecutive numbers by incrementing.
Track the maximum sequence length found.
common_mistakes: Sorting the array (O(n log n) instead of O(n))
Not checking if number is sequence start (leads to O(n²))
Recounting the same sequence multiple times
Using O(n²) nested loops instead of hash set
content.problem_description: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. The algorithm must run in O(n) time.

hints: Group arrays into two pairs: (nums1, nums2) and (nums3, nums4).
Compute all possible sums from first pair, store in hashmap with counts.
For each sum from second pair, check if its negation exists in hashmap.
Count total tuples by multiplying frequencies.
common_mistakes: Using O(n⁴) bruteforce instead of O(n²) hashmap approach
Not using counts in hashmap (missing duplicate combinations)
Incorrectly grouping arrays for optimal performance
Integer overflow when computing sums
content.problem_description: Given four integer arrays, return the number of tuples (i, j, k, l) such that nums1[i] + nums2[j] + nums3[k] + nums4[l] = 0.

learningAid.title: QuickSelect Algorithm
learningAid.explanation: QuickSelect is a selection algorithm to find the kth smallest/largest element in O(n) average time. It uses partitioning logic similar to QuickSort but only recurses into one partition containing the target element.

hints: Find the first decreasing element from the right (pivot).
Find the smallest element greater than pivot to its right.
Swap them, then reverse the suffix to get smallest arrangement.
If no pivot found, reverse the entire array.
common_mistakes: Not correctly identifying the pivot element
Not finding the smallest greater element in the suffix
Forgetting to reverse the suffix after swapping
Handling the case when array is already in descending order incorrectly
content.problem_description: Given an array of integers nums, rearrange it into the next lexicographically greater permutation. If no such permutation exists, rearrange it to the lowest possible order.

hints: For QuickSelect: use partitioning like QuickSort but only recurse into one partition.
For Min Heap: maintain a heap of size k containing the k largest elements.
For Sorting: sort descending and return element at index k-1.
QuickSelect is O(n) average but O(n²) worst case.
common_mistakes: Using O(n log n) sorting when O(n) QuickSelect is possible
Using max heap instead of min heap (less efficient for kth largest)
Incorrect partitioning logic in QuickSelect
Off-by-one errors in k indexing
content.problem_description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array.

problems.name: Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Space

hints: Use the gap method: start with gap = ceil((n+m)/2).
Compare elements i and i+gap, swap if out of order.
Reduce gap by half each iteration until gap becomes 1.
This is essentially Shell Sort on the concatenated array.
common_mistakes: Using extra space when in-place is required
Not correctly calculating the gap sequence
Off-by-one errors in index calculations
Using O(n*m) insertion sort instead of O((n+m) log(n+m))
content.problem_description: Given two sorted arrays arr1 and arr2 of sizes n and m respectively, merge them in-place into arr1 such that arr1 is sorted after merging.

hints: Use a min heap of size k+1.
Add first k+1 elements to the heap.
Extract minimum and add to result, then add next element.
This works because the minimum element must be within k+1 positions.
common_mistakes: Using O(n log n) sorting when O(n log k) is possible
Using wrong heap size (should be k+1 not k)
Not handling the case when k >= n
Using insertion sort for large k values (inefficient)
content.problem_description: Given an array of n elements where each element is at most k positions away from its sorted position, sort the array efficiently.

hints: Use modified merge sort: count inversions during merge step.
When merging, if element from right array is smaller than left, it forms inversions.
Count inversions as: number of remaining elements in left array.
The merge step then proceeds normally.
common_mistakes: Counting pairs during merge instead of before merge (wrong results)
Confusing this with count of inversions (condition is > 2*j not > j)
Not correctly handling the merge step after counting
Using O(n²) bruteforce for large arrays
content.problem_description: Given an array, count the number of inversions. An inversion is a pair of indices (i, j) such that i < j and arr[i] > arr[j].

hints: Binary search on the smaller array to find the correct partition.
Partition both arrays such that elements on left are <= elements on right.
For median: left partition should have (m+n+1)/2 elements total.
Check partition condition: maxLeft1 <= minRight2 and maxLeft2 <= minRight1.
common_mistakes: Using O(m+n) merge approach instead of O(log(min(m,n))) binary search
Not correctly calculating partition indices
Not handling edge cases when one array is fully included/excluded
Incorrect median calculation for even/odd total length
content.problem_description: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2 of size m and n respectively, return the median of the two sorted arrays with O(log (m+n)) time complexity.

problems.name: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

hints: Use modified merge sort: track original indices during sorting.
During merge, when element from right is smaller, count how many left elements are skipped.
Store counts using original indices after sorting is complete.
The merge step needs to handle the index mapping carefully.
common_mistakes: Using O(n²) bruteforce for large arrays
Not correctly tracking original indices during sorting
Incorrect count calculation during merge step
Complex index mapping between sorted and original arrays
content.problem_description: Given an integer array nums, return an array counts where counts[i] is the number of smaller elements to the right of nums[i].

learningAid.title: Binary Exponentiation
learningAid.explanation: Binary exponentiation computes x^n in O(log n) time by using the binary representation of n. Instead of multiplying x n times, we square x repeatedly and multiply only when the corresponding bit is set in n. This is essential for large exponents.

hints: Use binary exponentiation: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2 if n is even, else x * (x^(n/2))^2.
Handle negative exponents by computing 1 / pow(x, -n).
Use recursion or iterative approach with bit manipulation.
Be careful with integer overflow in intermediate calculations.
common_mistakes: Using O(n) linear multiplication instead of O(log n) binary exponentiation
Not handling negative exponents correctly
Integer overflow when computing intermediate results
Stack overflow for very large n in recursive approach
content.problem_description: Implement pow(x, n), which calculates x raised to the power n (i.e., x^n).

hints: DP: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1] (paths from top + paths from left).
Combinatorics: answer = C(m+n-2, m-1) = (m+n-2)! / ((m-1)! * (n-1)!).
Optimize DP space by using only one row instead of full matrix.
